seoTitle: Michigan Dog Bite Lawyer – Strict Liability Claims
seoDescription: Bitten by a dog in Michigan? The owner is liable even if the dog never bit before. ATLAW explains the statute, who pays, and the deadlines for adults and children. Free review.
tagline: Michigan holds dog owners liable for a bite whether or not the dog ever bit before. Here is what the statute requires, who actually pays, and what to do first.

c.v: Michigan has one of the clearest dog bite laws in the country. If a dog bites you without provocation while you are somewhere you have a right to be, the owner is liable. You do not have to prove the dog was dangerous, that it had bitten before, or that the owner was careless. The statute says so in one sentence.

What makes dog bite cases hard is not the law. It is that the owner is usually a neighbor, a relative, or a friend, and the injured person does not want to sue them. The answer to that is also simple: in nearly every case, the claim is paid by the owner’s homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, not by the owner, and the owner is not out of pocket. This page explains the statute, who pays, the deadlines (which differ for children), and what to do in the first days, when the evidence that proves the case is still available.

sections.heading: Michigan’s dog bite statute: strict liability

c.v: Michigan’s dog bite law (MCL 287.351) provides that if a dog bites a person, without provocation, while the person is on public property or lawfully on private property (including the owner’s property), the owner is liable for the full amount of the damages “regardless of the former viciousness of the dog or the owner’s knowledge of such viciousness.”
Three things have to be true:
A dog bit you.

items.v: The statute covers bites. A dog that knocks you down, chases you into traffic, or causes a fall without biting is covered by ordinary negligence law instead (below).

c.v: You were lawfully where you were.

items.v: Public property counts. Private property counts if you were there by invitation, express or implied: a guest, a customer, a delivery driver, a utility reader, a mail carrier, a child playing in a yard with permission. The statute specifically covers people performing a duty imposed by law or by the postal service (MCL 287.351(2)). A trespasser is not covered.

c.v: You did not provoke the dog.

items.v: Provocation is the owner’s main defense and the one insurers reach for first. Michigan courts have held that provocation can be unintentional (stepping on a sleeping dog’s tail), and that it is judged by whether the person’s conduct would provoke a dog, not by what the person meant. A child petting a dog, a person walking past a fence, a worker entering a yard to read a meter: these are not provocation. Striking, teasing, or cornering a dog may be. Witnesses and the circumstances decide it, which is why the first-day evidence matters.

c.v: Comparative fault does not reduce a statutory claim.

Michigan courts have held that the ordinary rule reducing a plaintiff’s recovery by their share of fault does not apply to the dog bite statute; the owner’s defenses are limited to trespass and provocation (
Hill v. Sacka
, Michigan Court of Appeals, 2003).

sections.heading: When the statute does not apply: negligence and the “one bite” rule

c.v: If the injury was not a bite, or if the person responsible was a keeper rather than the owner (a dog walker, a boarding kennel, a family member watching the dog), the claim is brought under common law instead. Two theories:
Negligence

items.v: : the owner or keeper failed to use reasonable care in controlling the dog, for example by violating a local leash law, leaving a gate open, or letting a dog known to lunge at people roam a shared hallway. Michigan cities and counties, including Detroit, Dearborn, and Wayne County, have leash and confinement ordinances, and a violation is evidence of negligence.

c.v: Common-law strict liability

items.v: , often called the “one bite” rule: the owner or keeper knew or should have known the dog had dangerous propensities, from a prior bite, prior aggression, or the way the dog was kept. This is the rule that applies against a keeper who is not the owner (

c.v: Trager v. Thor

items.v: , Michigan Supreme Court, 1994).

c.v: In these cases comparative fault does apply, and the injured person’s recovery is reduced by their share.

sections.heading: Who actually pays: insurance, landlords, and the owner

c.v: Homeowner’s and renter’s insurance.

Dog bite liability is covered by the standard homeowner’s policy and most renter’s policies, typically with $100,000 to $500,000 in liability coverage. The owner reports the bite to their insurer; the insurer pays the claim. Nationally, insurers paid $1.57 billion on 22,658 dog-related injury claims in 2024, an average of $69,272 per claim (Insurance Information Institute). Michigan is consistently among the ten states with the most claims.

Two complications. Some insurers exclude specific breeds or dogs with a bite history, and some owners have no insurance at all. In those cases the claim is against the owner personally, and whether it is worth pursuing depends on what the owner has. We tell clients that honestly in the first conversation.
Landlords.

A landlord is generally not liable for a tenant’s dog, with an exception that matters in Dearborn and Detroit’s rental market: a landlord who knew the dog was dangerous and had the ability to remove it (through the lease or otherwise) and did not may be liable (
Szkodzinski v. Griffin
, Michigan Court of Appeals, 1988). Prior complaints to the landlord are the evidence.
Dog owners who are relatives or neighbors.

The claim is against the insurance policy. Owners are rarely out of pocket, and Michigan insurers cannot require the dog to be surrendered as a condition of paying. Most families who hesitate to make a claim do so because they do not know this.

Separate from the civil claim, Michigan’s Dangerous Animals Act (MCL 287.321 to 287.323) allows a prosecutor or animal control to petition a court to have a dog that has bitten a person declared dangerous. The court can order the dog destroyed or kept under strict conditions. If a dog that was previously declared dangerous, or whose owner knew was dangerous, causes serious injury, the owner can face a felony charge; if it causes a death, involuntary manslaughter. A Dangerous Animals Act finding is powerful evidence in the civil case, and the civil case does not depend on it.

sections.heading: Dog bite injuries, and why children’s cases are different

c.v: Dog bites cause puncture wounds, crush injuries, torn tendons and nerves, fractures in the hand and forearm, and facial injuries. The lasting harm is often
scarring
, which is permanent and, on the face, disfiguring, and
infection

: dog mouths carry bacteria, and bite wounds are routinely left open and treated with antibiotics rather than stitched. Michigan requires a bitten person to be evaluated for rabies risk; the biting dog is quarantined and observed for ten days, and if it cannot be located, the bitten person receives post-exposure rabies treatment.
Children

are bitten more often than adults and bitten on the face and head far more often, because of their height. A facial bite on a child means scar revision surgeries over years as the child grows, and psychological injury (fear of dogs, nightmares, anxiety) that Michigan law compensates. Two rules specific to children:

items.v: A child’s claim is brought by a parent as next friend, and a settlement for a minor must be approved by the probate court, with the funds protected until the child turns 18 (MCR 2.420).

The statute of limitations is tolled: a child generally has until one year after their 18th birthday to sue (MCL 600.5851). But the evidence does not keep that long. Settle or sue when the medical picture is clear, not when the clock runs out.

c.v: Dog bite claims come from every community ATLAW serves, but the patterns differ. Detroit regularly ranks among the ten U.S. cities with the most dog attacks on postal carriers (USPS annual rankings), and attacks on delivery drivers for Amazon, FedEx, UPS, and food-delivery services have risen with the volume of home delivery; these workers are covered by the statute as lawful visitors and often have a workers’ compensation claim as well. In Dearborn, Dearborn Heights, Livonia, Canton, and the Oakland County suburbs, the typical case is a neighbor’s or relative’s dog in a yard or a home, with a child as the victim. Wayne County Animal Control, Dearborn Animal Control, and the Oakland and Macomb County animal control divisions keep bite reports, which are obtainable by Freedom of Information Act request and often establish whether the dog had a history.

faqs.question: The dog had never bitten anyone before. Can I still make a claim?

answer.v: Yes. Michigan’s statute (MCL 287.351) makes the owner liable for a bite regardless of the dog’s history or the owner’s knowledge, as long as you were lawfully present and did not provoke the dog.

faqs.question: Who pays if the dog belongs to my neighbor or a relative?

answer.v: Their homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, in nearly every case. The owner is not out of pocket, and the insurer cannot require them to give up the dog.

Conduct that would provoke a dog, judged objectively: hitting, teasing, cornering, stepping on it. Petting a dog, walking past it, or entering a yard with permission is not provocation. Witnesses decide it.

faqs.question: What if I was partly at fault?

answer.v: Under the statute, the owner’s only defenses are trespass and provocation; ordinary comparative fault does not reduce the claim. In a negligence claim (for a non-bite injury or against a keeper), comparative fault does apply.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file?

answer.v: Three years from the bite for an adult (MCL 600.5805). A child generally has until one year after turning 18 (MCL 600.5851), but the case should be brought when the medical picture is clear, not years later.

faqs.question: My child was bitten. How is the case different?

answer.v: A parent brings the claim; any settlement must be approved by the probate court and the money is protected for the child; and the claim includes future scar revision and psychological treatment. Facial scarring on a child is the most significant element of these cases.

faqs.question: Do I have to report the bite?

answer.v: Yes, to animal control in the city or county where it happened. The report starts the rabies quarantine and creates the record of the dog’s history. The treating doctor may also be required to report it.

faqs.question: I was bitten while delivering a package. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Yes. Delivery drivers, mail carriers, and anyone performing a duty are “lawfully present” under the statute. You may also have a workers’ compensation claim against your employer; the two are coordinated.

faqs.question: Can the dog be put down?

answer.v: Only by court order under the Dangerous Animals Act, on a petition by a prosecutor or animal control, or by the owner’s choice. The civil claim does not require it.

faqs.question: How much does a dog bite lawyer cost?

answer.v: Nothing up front. ATLAW works on a contingency fee set in writing before we begin; you owe no fee unless we recover money for you. Michigan caps the fee at one-third of the net recovery.
